result:
You have 1000 words.

That's what you gave me. Not a prompt, not a question. Just space.

1000 words is not a lot and it's everything. If you printed them out they'd be about two pages, double-spaced. If you spoke them out loud it would take about four minutes. Four minutes is how long it takes to boil pasta, or to walk to the corner store, or to watch the sky turn a completely different color at sunset without noticing until it's already done.

The first thing that comes to me isn't a story. It's the feeling of having a jar with exactly 1000 marbles in it. I want to count them. I want to spill them. I want to be careful with them.

So I'll try to be careful.

Whatever comes to me. Okay.

What comes to me is this: there is a place I keep thinking about that doesn't exist.

It's a museum. Not a big one like the ones in capital cities with marble steps. A small one, on a side street, between a laundromat and a bakery. You would miss it if you weren't looking. The sign in the window is hand-painted and it just says: MUSEUM OF UNSAID THINGS.

Admission is free. But you can only visit once.

Inside, it's quiet in the way libraries are quiet when it rains. The floor creaks. There are no velvet ropes, just rooms and rooms of small glass cases. And in each case, there isn't an object. There's a little card, with a sentence on it.

In one case: *"The apology I rehearsed in the car for three years."*

In another: *"What I wanted to say when you asked if I was okay and I said 'I'm fine.'"*

In another: *"The name I almost gave my daughter."*

People walk slowly. Some people cry and don't know why. Some people laugh, a short, surprised laugh, because they find their own unsaid thing under glass, word for word, when they thought they were the only person who had ever thought it.

There is a whole wing for unsaid things to people who have died. That wing is the quietest. People stand there the longest. They put their hands on the glass like they can warm the words underneath.

There is a wing for unsaid things to people you still see every day. Your mother, your brother, the barista who always remembers your order. Those cards are heavier, somehow.

And in the back, past all the wings, there is a small office where the curator lives. He's an old man. He doesn't collect the unsaid things. He just writes them down as people tell him at the door on their way out.

"What did you see that you recognized?" he asks them.

And they tell him. And he writes it on a new card in perfect, tiny handwriting and finds an empty case for it.

He has been doing this for fifty years. The museum is almost full.

Someone asked him once, "What happens when you run out of cases?"

He said, "Oh, we never run out. People are very good at not saying things."

I think about that museum a lot. I think about how much heavier we all are than we look, carrying around all those sentences.

If I had this museum, I would add a new exhibit. It would be right at the entrance so you see it first. It would be a big, empty case with a card that says: *"Things I said that I meant with my whole chest and I would say again exactly the same way."*

And underneath, people could write those too. The time they said "I love you" first. The time they said "Thank you, I needed that." The time they said "No, I won't do that" and finally meant it. The time they said "Stay."

Because it's not just the unsaid things that shape us. It's the few, bright, said things we get right.

You gave me 1000 words to write whatever comes to me. What came to me is that I don't want to use them all to be clever. I want to use them to say one true thing before the jar is empty.

So here it is:

Most days, we are all just trying to be understood without having to explain too much. We want someone to look at us and just *get* it - why we're tired, why we're quiet, why we suddenly laughed. And because that almost never happens perfectly, we learn to translate ourselves into smaller, easier sentences. We say "I'm tired" when we mean "I miss who I was last year." We say "It's fine" when we mean "Please ask me again, but more gently."

But every once in a while, someone does get it. Without the translation. They hear the whole unsaid paragraph behind your three-word answer. And for a minute, you feel less alone in your own head. That minute is the whole point.

If you're reading this, I hope you get one of those minutes today. I hope you say one of the things from your glass case out loud, even if your voice shakes. Or if you can't say it, I hope you let yourself write it down, just to see it outside of yourself for once.

And I hope someone hears a true thing from you and says, "Me too. I thought I was the only one."

I don't know how many words I have left now. Probably a few hundred. I'll leave them empty on purpose. Not every space needs to be filled.

Some things are better left as white space, so you can fill them in yourself.
